ground: The ayah names the straight road asked for in 1:6. It is the road of those on whom You have bestowed favor, not of those on whom anger has come, nor of those who have gone astray. Three groups are set side by side. The first is the favored, whose favor comes directly from 'You'. The second is those on whom anger has fallen; no one is named as the one who is angry. The third is those who themselves have lost the way. The prayer, and the surah, end with the request to be on the first road and kept from the other two conditions.

triggers.how: the same noun repeated: 1:7:1 stands in apposition (badal) to the road of 1:6
the repeated road is now made definite by the people who walked it
perfect tense: the favor has already been given and the road already walked

findings.statement: The straight road of 1:6 is named a second time. This time it is identified by the people who were favored on it, and their favor is already complete (past tense).
findings.perceptible: The road becomes peopled and historical. Its description is not what identifies it. The one praying asks to follow a track that others have already walked and been favored on.

triggers.how: 4:68 has the same verb hadā with ṣirāṭan mustaqīman, and 4:69 continues with alladhīna anʿama Allāhu ʿalayhim: an explaining passage that repeats the whole sequence of 1:6–7
4:69 lists them as prophets, the truthful, witnesses and the righteous, and closes with wa-ḥasuna ulāʾika rafīqā

findings.statement: 4:68–69 unfolds the same phrase in the same order. Read with it, the road of those You favored is also a road walked with those people as companions.
findings.perceptible: The road becomes relational. The one praying asks to join a company of walkers, not only to be given a direction. The dictionary here does not cover rafīq, so 'companion on the road' rests on memory.

triggers.how: the canonical sirāṭa reading brings out yastariṭu sālikahu, the road that takes its walker in
ض ل ل B002: to vanish into something else or into the ground; aḍalla al-mayyit means to bury the dead
the same road with the same swallowing branch

findings.statement: The ayah contrasts the road of the favored with straying. Its first and last words can also be heard as two ways of disappearing. One is being taken into the road and carried along it. The other is vanishing into the waste.
findings.perceptible: It gives the ayah a spatial frame from its first word to its last. The walker is absorbed either way, either by the road or by the empty land. Staying on the road is what keeps the walker from being lost.

triggers.how: the branches B001–B005 together: missing the way, vanishing, a thing gone from its owner or a place one cannot find, loss of memory, a beast lost in the waste
the entries define ḍalāl as the opposite of hudā

findings.statement: Those who have gone astray are those who have lost the way. All the branches of the root share one idea: being gone from the place where one could be found. This covers a road missed, an animal gone from its owner, something forgotten, a body buried, and blood that no one avenged.
findings.perceptible: Straying stops being only a moral deviation and becomes a condition of being lost to someone. It is losing contact, not only choosing wrongly.

triggers.how: the entry defines the ḍālla as the camel left in a wasteland 'whose rabb is not known' (lā yuʿrafu rabbuhā); the same word the surah uses for God
the owner's brand (wasm), the mark by which an animal is known as someone's
hādī, the lead animal at the front of the herd
ن ع م B005 naʿam/anʿām, the herd itself, a word of the same root placed just before ḍāllīn

findings.statement: Those who go astray lose the road. In the herd scene the surah has built, they are also the stray beast whose rabb no one knows, and al-Jawharī's 'ḍill ibn ḍill' describes someone who is not known and whose father is not known.
findings.perceptible: The last word points back to the surah's first words. Belonging, a Lord who raises, and a guide at the front all come before it, and the surah ends by asking not to become the beast without a known owner. Straying is shown as loss of belonging.

triggers.how: 15:56: 'who despairs of the mercy (raḥma) of his rabb except the ḍāllūn'. The same lemma is joined to raḥma and rabb
93:7: 'He found you ḍāll and guided (hadā)'. The same lemma answered by the verb of 1:6

findings.statement: The ḍāllīn are those who have lost the way. Elsewhere the same word describes those who no longer see their Lord's mercy (15:56), and the Prophet himself, once lost and then found and guided (93:7).
findings.perceptible: Straying is not presented as a fixed identity. It is a state of being out of sight of the rabb and the raḥma named at the start of the surah, and guidance can reach someone in that state.

triggers.how: Maqāyis: the root is 'a sound origin indicating hardness and strength'. Ghaḍba is hard rock, and ghaḍab is said to be derived from it as 'the intensifying of displeasure'. Other branches: thick skin (B005) and hard folded hide used like a shield (B008)

findings.statement: Those on whom anger has come meet anger. According to Ibn Fāris the word itself is built on hardness: displeasure made firm like rock.
findings.perceptible: Anger becomes something material: a hardening of displeasure, the opposite of riḍā. It is not a passing emotional outburst, as the Turkish 'gazap' may suggest.

triggers.how: ghaḍba rock (B004), thick skin (B005), hard hide (B008) against naʿuma, 'to become soft' (B002)
the same 'upon them' follows both verbs, so the two parts stand as a pair

findings.statement: The ayah sets favor against anger. Underneath, it sets softness against hardness: the favored are given life that is soft and easy (naʿuma, niʿma), while the others meet something hard as rock (ghaḍba).
findings.perceptible: It gives the contrast a physical, tactile quality. The favor is felt as ease and softness of condition, and the anger is felt as meeting rock.

triggers.how: active verb, second person: 'You favored'. It continues the direct address that began with iyyāka in 1:5
active participle: those who themselves stray

findings.statement: The three groups are named in three different grammatical ways. The favor is attributed directly to 'You'. The anger is a passive participle with no named agent. The straying is the strayers' own act.
findings.perceptible: The words spoken to God keep 'You' for the giving. Anger is described only as something that has come upon people, and straying is described as something people do. A Turkish translation that says 'gazabına uğrayanlar' (those who met Your anger) adds a 'Your' that the Arabic does not have.

triggers.how: the same preposition and pronoun repeated after the anger word
the third group has no ʿalā

findings.statement: Favor and anger both come 'upon them' (ʿalayhim ... ʿalayhim). The third group has nothing coming upon them; they are simply the ones who have gone astray.
findings.perceptible: There is a vertical structure. Favor and anger descend onto people, while the strayers have nothing over them and move sideways into the waste. This matches the idea of straying as going out of reach.

triggers.how: the branches together: a good condition and a good life (B001), softness and ease (B002), doing something thoroughly (B010), a land that suits one and where staying is pleasant (B011), 'God made your eye glad' (B013)

findings.statement: The favored have been given good. The root's branches share one idea: a condition made soft, pleasant and complete, including a place where one settles well and a gladness of the eye.
findings.perceptible: Niʿma is a state one is placed in, not a list of possessions or food. Anʿamta means 'You made their condition good'.

triggers.how: a request that waits for an answer
a request for help

findings.statement: Those You favored are those given good. The same verb (anʿama lahu) also means 'said naʿam, yes, to him', so the favored can also be heard as those whose request was answered with yes. The dictionary attests this sense with the preposition la-, while the ayah uses ʿalā.
findings.perceptible: The prayer of 1:5–6 ends by naming a group that was answered yes. This gives the petition a hope of being answered, set inside the word itself.

triggers.how: praise and thanks that answer a favor; it stands at the start and the favor is named at the end
hadiyya: a gift sent gently
27:19 and 46:15 use the same second-person form in a prayer: 'that I may thank Your favor which You bestowed (anʿamta) upon me'

findings.statement: The favor named here completes the thanks the surah began with. Elsewhere the Quran uses this same 'anʿamta' in prayers that ask for the ability to give thanks.
findings.perceptible: There is a circle in the surah's composition: the ḥamd in 1:2 comes before the favor is named, and the favor is named only here. Anʿamta is the natural word of a thankful person speaking to God.

triggers.how: 8:53 joins the two roots: God does not change (mughayyiran) a favor He bestowed (anʿamahā) on a people until they change (yughayyirū) what is in themselves
ghayr stands between the favored and the others

findings.statement: Ghayr marks the others off from the favored: 'not those'. Its root also means changing and exchanging, and 8:53 uses it beside anʿama for a favor that can be changed.
findings.perceptible: The line between the groups can be heard as a line that can be crossed. The prayer asks both to be on the road and to stay on it.

triggers.how: 2:40, 2:47 and 2:122: 'remember My favor which I bestowed (anʿamtu) upon you'. The favor is something to be remembered

findings.statement: The ḍāllīn are those who have lost the way. The root also means losing something from memory, and the Quran's repeated call to 'remember My favor' sets remembering the favor against that forgetting.
findings.perceptible: It links the first group and the last one in time. The favor is kept by remembering it, and straying can start as forgetting.

triggers.how: the branches together: swallowing a morsel easily (B002), the road (B001), the sword that goes through its stroke (B003)

findings.statement: Ṣirāṭ is a road. All its branches share the idea of passing through without obstruction: food down a throat, a traveler along a road, a blade through its cut.
findings.perceptible: The road is felt as easy passage, something a person moves through rather than struggles against.

triggers.how: the mutawātir reading sirāṭa, with sīn

findings.statement: In the canonical sirāṭa reading the word means the road. With sīn it also sounds out sarata, 'to swallow', and al-sirāṭ as the road that takes its walker in.
findings.perceptible: It supports F3 and F16 through recited sound, not through a guess about etymology.

triggers.how: the Turkish reader hears 'sırat köprüsü', described in Turkish as 'kıldan ince, kılıçtan keskin' (thinner than a hair, sharper than a sword)

findings.statement: Here ṣirāṭ is the road of the favored. The dictionary's own branch of ṣirāṭ as a sharp, cutting sword explains why the word could later carry the image of a blade-like bridge.
findings.perceptible: The reader's association with the bridge is recognized and placed correctly, so they are not confused. In this ayah the word is a road walked in company, not the bridge of the hereafter.

triggers.how: غ ض ب B001–B002: anger rising for revenge; being angry for a living man or on behalf of a dead one
ض ل ل B003: blood that is lost with no one avenging it
the Day on which what is owed is settled

findings.statement: The last three content words have their plain sense. Beneath it, each also belongs to the vocabulary of blood feud: blood-money paid instead of retaliation, rising for revenge, and blood left unavenged.
findings.perceptible: It is a faint echo of the settling of debts on the Day of 1:4, placed at the surah's end.

triggers.how: the road leads to a place
B012 tanaʿʿama: to come or seek on foot

findings.statement: The favored have been given good. Through tanaʿʿamatnī al-arḍ ('the land suited me and I settled there'), their favor can also be heard as arriving at a place where staying is good.
findings.perceptible: The road has an end point, a lodging where one stays well.

triggers.how: submission set against defiance in the rule.obedience scene

findings.statement: Those on whom anger has come are met with anger. The root's sense of mughāḍaba, defying and opposing someone, lets one hear a relationship of opposition behind it.
findings.perceptible: The anger is heard as belonging to a quarrel between two sides, set against the service declared in 1:5.

triggers.how: the negation lā is repeated after ghayr
ghayri is genitive, agreeing with alladhīna

findings.statement: Ghayri is in the genitive, following alladhīna. It can describe the favored themselves as not being among the angered or the astray, or it can mark a second group. The repeated lā keeps the two excluded groups separate.
findings.perceptible: The favored are identified both by what they received and by what they are not. The two dangers are not merged into one.

triggers.how: sound: the long ā before a doubled lām, recited with the longest obligatory lengthening (madd lāzim)

findings.statement: The last word of the surah names those who have strayed. In recitation it is also the most drawn-out word of the surah.
findings.perceptible: The word's length in time echoes a long wandering. It is felt in recitation, not read.

triggers.how: 2:40, 2:47 and 2:122 address Banū Isrāʾīl as recipients of anʿamtu

findings.statement: Traditional exegesis and a hadith often give names to the angered and the astray. The ayah itself names them by what has come upon them and what they did, so the description stays open as a warning to whoever prays these words.
findings.perceptible: The identifications in the commentary tradition are recorded here without narrowing the plain wording.

loaded_words.role: A route toward which people are guided or invited, or which they follow or stay on; most often ṣirāṭ mustaqīm, linked to hadā and ittabaʿa
loaded_words.departure: Turkish 'sırat' first suggests the bridge over hell. Here, as in almost all Quranic uses, it is a road that people walk and are guided onto.

loaded_words.role: Always with ʿalā; the giver is God (in 33:37 once also the Prophet). The favor bestowed calls for remembrance and thanks (2:40, 2:47, 2:122, 27:19, 46:15), and people turn away from it (17:83, 41:51). Those favored include prophets and the righteous (4:69, 19:58)
loaded_words.count: 17 of 17 with ʿalā; 16 of 17 with God as the giver
loaded_words.departure: Turkish 'nimet' leans toward possessions, food and blessings as things. Here the verb names an act of making someone's condition good. Its recipients are persons.

loaded_words.role: A person lost from the way, often in someone's own confession or verdict ('I was among the ḍāllīn': 26:20, 2:198, 23:106). In 68:26 it is literally losing the way to a garden. In 93:7 it describes someone found and guided
loaded_words.count: 14 of 14 describe being lost or off course, several in self-description
loaded_words.departure: Turkish 'dalalet/sapkın' carries a heavy verdict of heresy. The Quranic uses include pardonable, recoverable lostness (Moses in 26:20, the Prophet in 93:7).

loaded_words.role: Occurs only here; a passive participle with no named agent
loaded_words.departure: Turkish translations often add 'Your' ('gazabına uğrayanlar'). The Arabic leaves the agent unnamed.

loaded_words.role: Names an alternative or other entity or group
loaded_words.departure: Turkish 'gayri' suggests 'artık' (anymore) or a negating prefix ('gayrimeşru'). Here it marks off other groups: 'not those'.

losses.loses: The plain sense of a road already walked by people, and the swallowing/passing-through branch (the road that takes its walker in)
losses.adds: The bridge over hell, 'kıldan ince kılıçtan keskin' (thinner than a hair, sharper than a sword): an image of a test and of fear, not of a road walked in company

losses.loses: Softness and ease of condition, 'saying yes', a place that suits one, and gladness of the eye; the favor as a state one is placed in
losses.adds: The everyday sense of nimet as food and material goods ('nimete saygı')

losses.loses: The root's hardness (rock, thick hide), anger as the opposite of riḍā, and the passive voice with no agent
losses.adds: An emotional outburst of rage. In the 'gazabına' form, an explicit 'Your' that the Arabic does not state

losses.loses: The lost beast whose owner is unknown, vanishing, forgetting, a thing gone from its owner; lostness that can be found again
losses.adds: 'Sapık' and 'sapkın' carry ideological or sexual deviance and social stigma, and 'dalalet' a heavy doctrinal charge of heresy

losses.loses: The root's sense of change and exchange, which 8:53 uses beside anʿama
losses.adds: Colloquial 'gayri' = 'artık' (anymore); the reader may also confuse it with 'gayret' (effort), a false friend from the same root (jealous protection)

grammar: ṣirāṭa (1:7:1) stands in apposition to al-ṣirāṭa al-mustaqīma of 1:6. The same road is named again, this time by its walkers.

anʿamta is active, second person ('You favored'); al-maghḍūbi ʿalayhim is a passive participle with no agent; al-ḍāllīna is an active participle (they themselves stray). The Arabic does not say 'Your anger'.
ʿalayhim is repeated with both favor and anger, so both 'come upon' people. The strayers have no ʿalā.

ghayri is genitive, following alladhīna. It either describes the favored as not being the angered or the astray, or it adds a second group. wa-lā repeats the negation and keeps the two excluded groups distinct.
variants: sirāṭa (with sīn, mutawātir): makes the root's 'swallowing / taking in' sense audible. It supports hearing the road as one that takes its walker in (F3, F16).
ṣᶻirāṭa (ishmām, mutawātir): a transitional articulation between ṣād and sīn. It keeps the two sounds together and opens no separate reading.
reread: The road asked for in 1:6 is named again, and this time it is identified by people. It has been walked by those whose condition You made soft and good, and 4:69 shows them walking it as companions. The favor, spoken to 'You', finally names the gift that the ḥamd at the surah's opening had already answered. Against it stands an anger with no named agent. That anger comes upon people just as the favor does, and its root speaks of the hardness of rock, set against the softness of niʿma. Last come those who have lost the way. They have nothing coming upon them; they drift off into the waste like the camel whose rabb no one knows. Their lostness is losing touch with the Lord named at the start. Yet 93:7 shows that such a stray can still be found and guided, and ghayr, whose root means change, reminds the one praying that staying on the road is part of what they ask for.

set_aside.what: س ر ط ~alt B006–B008 (the crab, the constellation Cancer, the disease sarṭān) and B003 (sweet fālūdhaj)
set_aside.why: They are activated only by the scene grouping. Nothing in the ayah or the surah brings an animal, a star, an illness or a sweet into view.

set_aside.what: ن ع م B006–B008: ostrich; things likened to the ostrich; shālat naʿāmatuhum (they scattered or lost their strength)
set_aside.why: The dispersal idiom could echo straying, but no word in the ayah activates the ostrich. It is kept only as a scene echo, and ḍ-l-l already carries that sense better.

set_aside.what: ن ع م B009 al-nuʿāmā, the soft south wind
set_aside.why: It is one more member of the softness concept (F8, F11) and adds nothing of its own.

set_aside.what: غ ض ب B006 (swelling of the eyelid) and B007 (frowning; the great snake)
set_aside.why: Nothing in the neighbourhood supplies an eye or a snake. 1:6:3's eye scene is too weak to carry them.

set_aside.what: غ ض ب B002: being angry for a living person and on behalf of a dead one
set_aside.why: It appears only as a member of the vengeance scene (F19). By itself it gives no reading of maghḍūb ʿalayhim.

set_aside.what: غ ي ر B001 (provisioning the household, rain, fixing a saddle) and B004 (jealous protection)
set_aside.why: Nothing activates provision or rain here. B004 appears only in the losses entry as the source of the Turkish false friend 'gayret'.
It is not in the variant list given. Recalled from memory only, so it is not used.
They are purely phonetic and open no reading.

set_aside.what: The idea that the maghḍūb are hardened themselves (thick-skinned, frowning)
set_aside.why: Grammatically maghḍūb is the one on whom anger falls. The hardness belongs to the anger that meets them, and F7, F8 and F21 stay within that grammar.
